To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
crossmodal object recognition involves the activation of multisensory zones and that this activation is modality-dependent.

the perception of objects in one modality (e.g., vision) can be facilitated by the perception of the same objects in other modalities (e.g., touch or hearing) and that the brain mechanisms of this facilitation can be investigated using fMRI.
visual, tactile and auditory information about an object can activate cortical association zones that were previously believed to be modally specific.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional neuroimaging of crossmodal object recognition.
the question how the human brain processes information across the sensory modalities and how this information is integrated to form a representation of the object world.
the functional imaging of the human brain during crossmodal object recognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human brain is a highly flexible system for crossmodal object identification.
crossmodal interactions between sensory modalities are ubiquitous and can be observed at all levels of the processing hierarchy, from early sensory to high-level association cortex.
the human brain has the ability to integrate information from different sensory modalities to form a single representation of the external world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human brain is able to process information across sensory modalities, which allows the recognition of objects even if only one sensory modality is available.
the human brain is able to integrate sensory information from different modalities to recognize objects in an efficient way.
crossmodal processing of object information is not restricted to multisensory areas, but can be observed in many cortical areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human brain can integrate information from different sensory modalities to recognize objects.

crossmodal interactions are not limited to a few specialized brain regions but are a general feature of the cortical architecture that is crucial for the perception and recognition of objects in everyday life.
object perception is not limited by the sensory modalities that provide information about the object, but that the brain is able to integrate this information in a flexible way.
